paper_title: On-Policy Codec Distillation for Efficient All-in-One Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Modern visual generative models operate on tokens, and every visual asset they receive, whether an identity, a scribble, a depth map, or a motion video, is tokenized and appended to the input token sequence. Consequently, conditioning quickly dominates the computation cost. Yet most of these tokens carry redundant spatiotemporal information. Our key insight is that identifying what is genuinely new is exactly the problem that classical video codecs have long solved. Thus, we first introduce a codec-based token pruning method that discards redundant tokens. Then, we propose an on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) strategy to train a DiT adapter capable of learning the codec pruning pattern well without quality degradation. Together, they form On-Policy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our own video diffusion model, where it prunes 66% of the condition tokens on average with almost no quality drop. Therefore, denoising becomes 2x faster, and the cache memory shrinks by up to 73% in KV cache mode. CodecOPSD also extends to other state-of-the-art pretrained image and video generative models, where its benefit grows further with more conditions, longer frames, and higher resolution.

Introduction Creativity rarely arrives in text alone. To turn an afternoon at home into video, creator brings photo of the living room sofa, sketch of the room around it, the poses of two people, picture of the family corgi, and its path scribbled across the floor (Fig. 1 left). State-of-the-art video generative models can receive all these conditions as input. However, modern generative models concatenate all condition tokens into one sequence [5, 29, 30] as inputs, so the attention cost grows quadratically with every added condition. Fine-grained controllability then leads to severe computational cost. Most existing acceleration methods speed up the denoiser through fewer sampling steps [76], FlashAttention [56], quantization [43], feature caching [40], or sparse attention [73]. We instead reduce the condition tokens at their source, which is orthogonal to and pluggable into these methods. Condition signals are highly compressible, since 1 static background repeats in every frame and motion path covers few pixels. In our daily life, every video we watch or store is compressed by video codec such as H.264 [70], which removes exactly this redundancy. These codecs are the product of decades of traditional video compression research: rule-based systems that run efficiently on nearly every phone, camera, and browser. For every pixel of every frame, codec records how it can be predicted from earlier frames, as motion vector, and what remains new, as residual. These signals thus provide natural rule for selecting condition tokens of every modality, from natural RGB images and videos to sketches, depth, and motion tracks. They can be computed in real time on CPU during training and inference. Turning this idea into working model takes two steps: selecting the right tokens and adapting the model to learn from them. First, raw codec signals cannot be used directly and need careful engineering. We resolve these issues, propose an algorithm to map the signals from pixels to VAE tokens, and adapt the selection to each modality. Second, pruning alone is not enough, as the model must learn the codec pattern for faithful generation. We observe that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) leaves clear gap to the dense model on codec-pruned conditions. We instead propose adapting the model to the pruned conditions through onpolicy self-distillation (OPSD) [82], which supervises the model on the states of its own rollouts rather than on noised ground truth [2]. Teacher and student are the same base model, but the teacher additionally sees the tokens dropped by codec pruning as inferable privileged information. The teacher turns these tokens into dense guidance at every state of the students own rollout. We name this method OnPolicy Codec Distillation (CodecOPSD). To demonstrate the effectiveness of CodecOPSD, we adapt it to 16 condition modalities in our video diffusion model, namely segmentation, bounding box, identity, sketch, edge, depth, surface normal, human pose, sparse and dense tracking, blurring, grayscale, first-last frame interpolation, continuation, inpainting, and outpainting. With quality close to the dense teacher, it drops 66% of the condition tokens on average, which speeds up denoising by up to 2.30 and shrinks up to 73% of the memory cost in KV cache mode. We further apply it to three state-ofthe-art models, namely MiniMax-H3 Reference-to-AudioVideo (Ref2VA) [44] for video generation, MiniMax-H3Image [45] for image generation, and Cosmos3 [1] for physical AI tasks. At similar quality, the denoising speedup keeps growing with the input scale, reaching 3.72 on MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA with more references, 3.06 on MiniMax-H3-Image at 20482, and 2.30 on Cosmos3, with consistent gains across tasks as diverse as controlto-video, video continuation, video-to-audio, and video-toaction generation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose codec pruning in controllable generation, which maps the motion vectors and residuals of standard H.264 codec from pixels to VAE token masks. We introduce CodecOPSD, where the teacher additionally sees the codec-pruned tokens as privileged information, leaving the student an information gap that is inferable and of the right size. We scale CodecOPSD to 16 condition modalities on our video diffusion model, and further extend it to the state-of-the-art all-in-one models MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA, MiniMax-H3-Image, and Cosmos3. We show that CodecOPSD outperforms other token pruning baselines and has consistent gains in denoising speed with consistent quality. 2. Related Work Controllable Video Generation. Early controllable image and video generators add one condition type at time, such as ControlNet [78], SparseCtrl [17], and AVControl [5]. Later, more works extend them to multiple conditions for richer creative expression [3, 51, 65, 85]. On the other hand, all-in-one models train one network on many condition types. VACE [27] injects unified condition module through context adapter, FullDiT [29] and EditVerse [30] place all inputs in one token sequence under selfattention, and UniVideo [69] and OmniWeaving [48] pair multimodal language model with the diffusion transformer. The recent MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [44] accepts several image and video conditions at the same time. These models mostly append conditions along the sequence rather than the channel dimension, so as users bring ever more references, quadratic attention dominates the cost. This is exactly the problem we are addressing in this work. In diffuToken-Pruning-based Compression in Vision. sion models, ToMe-SD [7] merges tokens inside the network, and FullDiT2 [19] keeps the condition tokens ranked highest by learned scoring network. Keep The Essentials [49] instead drops reference tokens before the network, at random or by DeepGaze [35] saliency. Another common practice is to downscale the condition, as in OminiControl2 [62], EasyControl [81], and AVControl [5]. In visionlanguage models, codec-based encoders such as OneVisionEncoder [63], Video-LaVIT [28], CoPE-VideoLM [55], CodecSight [52], and AdaCodec [22] read the motion vectors and residuals of the compressed stream to skip or compactly encode redundant patches. These VLM works target understanding, where dropping redundant patches rarely changes the answer, so they can prune aggressively. Controllable generation is inherently different, since the content of pruned token still appears in the output, which calls for 2 DiT model. In Sec. 3.4, we design the model training for CodecOPSD. Video Codec Preliminaries As shown in Fig. 2, video codec such as H.264 [70] predicts each block of pixels from reference block in the same frame or in past frames. While codec also involves transform, quantization, and entropy coding, these stages are not relevant to our method, and we focus on how the reference and the residual of each block are obtained. The codec divides the frames of video into two types: intra-coded frames (I-frames) and predictive frames (Pframes). An I-frame has no temporal reference and predicts each block from its neighbours within the same frame (Fig. 2a). P-frame predicts each block from previously coded frames, where the compression encoder finds the best match with classical block-matching search algorithms (Fig. 2b). This match is rarely exact, so the codec stores the residual, which is the difference between the ground-truth block and its best match (Fig. 2c). In summary, P-frame provides motion vector mt(p) and residual rt(p) for the block of each pixel p, while an I-frame provides residual and no motion vector. 3.2. Experiments Secs. 4.1 and 4.2 provide the implementation and evaluation details. Sec. 4.3 analyzes token dropping and speedup 5 4.1. Implementation details We build our own multi-condition video model as the main testbed of this work. It is relatively lightweight and not distilled, and its training data comes with ground truth, so it can be directly trained with SFT. This enables the extensive SFT comparisons in Tab. 1 and shows the versatility of our method across diverse visual controls, each with its own metric. Our model starts from pretrained 22B-parameter text-image-to-video DiT, and its condition tokens never attend to the noise tokens, so it supports KV cache [62]. For the first stage, it is initially trained with text and mix of 16 condition modalities, namely segmentation, bounding box, identity, sketch, edge, depth, surface normal, human pose, sparse and dense tracking, blurring, grayscale, frame interpolation, continuation, inpainting, and outpainting. Each training sample uses 1 to 5 of them. All token pruning methods in Tab. 1 are also based on these weights. In the second stage, it is trained with CodecOPSD for 2K steps on 16 H200 GPUs. Inference sampling uses 30 denoising steps, and CodecOPSD rolls out the first 8 of these 30 steps in training. Further implementation details are in the supplementary material. 4.2. Evaluation details Evaluation dataset. The test clips of our model experiments are randomly selected from 2,000-video pool of VidGen-1M [61], where each comes with its ground truth and we prepare the condition modalities needed. Besides its diffusion transformer (DiT) [50], every condition image passes through the vision encoder (ViT) of its vision-language model (VLM) [4]. Condition videos are passed to this ViT as images at 2 FPS rate. The vision tokens of the VLM can amount to 33% of the condition tokens in the DiT. Therefore, we prune both kinds of tokens with the same codec signals in single pass. sections.content: In this supplementary material, we provide additional details and results for the main paper, which are organized as follows. Supplement provides the implementation details of our multi-condition video model, built on pretrained 22B DiT. Supplement provides the implementation details of our video codec. Supplement provides the test data, metrics, and settings of all experiments. Supplement provides additional quantitative results of our multi-condition video model. condition video model. Supplement provides additional ablation studies. Supplement provides additional details and results on MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [44]. Supplement provides additional details and results on MiniMax-H3-Image [45]. Supplement provides additional details and results on Cosmos3-Nano [1]. Supplement discusses the limitations of our method. A. Implementation details This section extends Sec. 4.1 of the main paper with further implementation details. Our internal model. Our internal model is pretrained DiT with 22B parameters (Tab. S1), and Fig. S1 shows how our multi-condition model uses it. Its 6B audio branch is not loaded, which leaves 16B parameters for video-only generation in all of our results. Each condition token enters the DiT with σ = 0 and attends to the tokens of its own condition. Therefore, its keys and values are computed once and cached [62]. Our LoRA [23] is applied to the condition tokens. Our internal model also has an 8-step distilled version [76] with the same architecture, which supports the KV cache in the same way. The dense LoRA trained on our internal model works directly on this distilled version, so we use it as the teacher without further training. The student starts from the same LoRA and is trained with CodecOPSD for 2K steps, where every denoising step of the distilled version is supervised. We adopt this setting for the main example in Fig. 1, the speedup test in Fig. 4, and the privileged teacher study in Supp. F.1. Table S1. Our internal model. We list the components of our internal model, whose audio branch is not loaded.

This stage uses all condition tokens and runs for 50,000 steps on 48 GPUs with global batch size of 48. In Stage 2, each fine-tuned row of Tab. 1 starts from the dense model and is trained for 2K steps on the same data, with 49 frames at 480640 and global batch size of 16. The SFT baselines continue to train the dense LoRA with the flow matching loss [39] on the ground-truth clips, each with its own token selection method. For CodecOPSD, we copy the dense LoRA into trainable student and freeze the dense model as the teacher. Both the student rollout and the teacher target use single conditional prediction without classifier-free guidance (CFG) [21], while CFG is applied at inference. CodecOPSD is optimized with AdamW at learning rate of 104. During training, the student receives the tokens that remain after threshold-based pruning with the fixed thresholds of Tab. S2. Across the four base models, our training data is drawn from parts of OpenVid-1M [47], VidGen-1M [61], SpatialVID [66], DL3DV-10K [38], and DROID [33], together with images and additional clips from our internal data pool. Conditions. Besides the text prompt, each training sample draws 1 to 5 of the 16 condition modalities described in Sec. 4.1. Their labels are extracted offline from each clip, except for edge, blurring, and grayscale, which are computed on the fly during data loading. Object-level conditions include segmentation, bounding boxes, and identity. For segmentation, Qwen3-VL [4] locates the objects in the first frame with bounding boxes, from which SAM3 [8] tracks each object through the clip. S1 Figure S1. Architecture of our multi-condition model. (a) Noise tokens attend to all tokens, while each clean condition attends to its own tokens. (b) Therefore, the keys and values of the conditions are computed once with our LoRA at step 1 and reused in all later steps, where the noise tokens alone enter the DiT. The resulting masks are rendered in one colour per object, either filled or as outlines. Bounding boxes form separate modality and are rendered from the same masks. For identity, we create reference image of each object from its crop, either as single-view identity, which shows one view of the object, or as multi-view identity, which shows several views of the object in one image. Structural conditions include sketch, edge, depth, surface normals, and human pose. For sketch, we use either the line drawings of Informative Drawings [9] in the anime, contour, and open sketch styles, or the straight lines of M-LSD [15]. Edge is separate modality that uses Canny edges with random thresholds. Depth maps are predicted by the small model of Video Depth Anything [10] and normalized per clip without further smoothing, while surface normals are predicted by NormalCrafter [6]. For human pose, we render the whole-body keypoints of Sapiens-1B [34] as skeleton for each person tracked by SAM3. Motion conditions include sparse and dense tracking. For tracking, CoTracker3 [31] tracks grid of points through each clip. Sparse tracking, denoted as motion track in Tab. 1 and Fig. 5, renders 1 to 20 of the fastest points as coloured squares. Dense tracking instead renders all points, coloured by their first-frame position and depth as in Diffusion as Shader [16]. Pixel-level conditions include blurring, grayscale, frame interpolation, continuation, inpainting, and outpainting. For blurring, 70% of the clips are degraded by Gaussian blur with the kernel settings of Cosmos-Transfer1 [3] followed by down-up sampling, and the rest by disk, Gaussian, or box kernel, from which the model restores the sharp clip. For grayscale, the condition retains the luma of the clip, which the model then colourizes. For frame interpolation and continuation, we retain the first frame, the first and last frames, or other frames of the clip and fill the remaining frames with grey. Inpainting masks follow DeepFillv2 [77] and LaMa [60] or are obtained from SAM3, while outpainting masks follow M3DDM [13] and cover either the whole clip or the first frame alone. B. Video codec implementation details This section extends Secs. 3.1 and 3.2 of the main paper with the details of token pruning, the codec reader and its fixes, and the H.264 [70] encoding settings. B.1. Token pruning This subsection details the two pruning mechanisms introduced in Sec. 3.2. Rescaling with the condition size. Since motion vectors are measured in pixels, the same movement yields larger motion score at higher resolution. In contrast, the residual score is averaged over the pixels of each token and decreases when an image is enlarged, since the same detail then spreads over more pixels. Therefore, we define the thresholds of Eq. 2 at standard size and rescale them by the condition size , which can be formulated as: τm = τ 0 (cid:113) HW H0W0 , (cid:113) τr = τ 0 s0 max(s0,min(H,W )) , (8) and τ 0 where τ 0 are the base thresholds listed in Tab. S2, defined at the standard size H0 W0 = 480 640 and the standard short side s0 = 1,024, respectively. The base thresholds are fixed for each condition type, and the rescaling adapts them to the resolution of the condition. The residual rescaling applies to images with short side above s0. Priority-based sorting. Priority-based sorting ranks the tokens by the energy Ei = Ri (1 + λ Mi) of Eq. 3, where Ri and Mi are the percentile ranks of Ri and Mi among the tokens of the same condition, both in [0, 1], and λ weights the motion. In practice, we set λ = 1. The tokens with the lowest energy are dropped first until the target drop rate is reached. Since motion scales the energy of token by factor between 1 and 1 + λ, tokens with low residual tend to be dropped first, as the codec already predicts their content. When priority-based sorting follows threshold-based pruning, the ranks are computed among the tokens with bi = 1. S2 Figure S2. Codec fixes. Each row shows an input, followed by its codec signal and the tokens after codec pruning, without the corresponding fix on the left and with it on the right. The four fixes (a) set uncoded intra blocks to 128, (b) set uncoded inter blocks to 128, (c) read the residual from the luma plane of the decoder instead of an RGB conversion, and (d) treat skipped macroblocks as static. Without these fixes, flat regions and backgrounds are mistaken for new content, and their tokens are not dropped. B.2. Codec reader and fixes Choice of H.264. H.264 [70] partitions each frame into macroblocks of 16 16 pixels, so each token covers whole macroblocks, and its scores follow directly from them. In contrast, H.265 [59] and AV1 [18] select blocks of up to 64 64 and 128 128 pixels, respectively, through ratedistortion optimization. single block can thus span several tokens, which makes the token scores depend on the partition decisions of the encoder. AV1 also predicts with warped and overlapped block motion, so the motion of block can no longer be described by single displacement. H.264 is also the fastest to encode. At the fastest setting of each encoder, x264 encodes 49-frame 480 640 clip in 0.06 s, while x265 and the libaom AV1 encoder take 0.17 and 0.65 s, respectively. Codec reader. Our codec reader builds upon the H.264 decoder of OneVision-Encoder [63], which is patched to instead of the reconstructed frame. output While its default behaviour is suitable for reconstruction, it mistakes flat backgrounds and the interior of moving shapes the residual for new content, and these false positives lower the drop rate. As shown in Fig. S2, we remove these false positives with four fixes that apply to all conditions. (a) Uncoded intra blocks. An intra block without coded coefficients holds its prediction, which extrapolates the residual of neighbouring blocks across flat regions. We set these blocks to 128, which denotes zero residual, and this increases the drop rate of identity references from 14.4% to 74.8%. (b) Uncoded inter blocks. An inter block without coded coefficients, including skipped block, holds motioncompensated prediction that copies the residual of its reference frame, so the residual of earlier frames persists. We also set these blocks to 128, which increases the drop rate of condition videos from 70.4% to 77.0%. (c) Luma plane. We read the residual directly from the luma plane of the decoder. Converting the decoded frame to RGB would instead interpret its 4:4:4 chroma as 4:2:0, which shifts the zero level away from 128 and introduces false residual. (d) Skipped macroblocks. skipped macroblock carries the motion vector predicted from its neighbours, so the flat interior of moving mask appears to be moving. We export skip flag from the decoder and treat skipped macroblocks as static, which increases the drop rate of condition videos from 74.6% to 77.0%. B.3. H.264 encoding settings In our simplified setting, an H.264 encoder codes the first frame of condition as an I-frame from its own pixels and each subsequent frame as P-frame. Each P-frame is predicted from reference frame with one motion vector per block, and the remaining prediction error is coded as the residual. The constant rate factor (CRF) controls how coarsely this residual is quantized, where higher CRF removes more small residuals. The preset controls how much effort the encoder spends on its decisions, such as the motion search and the number of reference frames. Presets. We adopt the fast presets in Tab. S2 for two reasons. First, they encode quickly, so codec pruning finishes before the GPU work on average for all four base models, as shown in Tab. S3. Second, they search small motion range over single reference, which is the previous frame. In contrast, slower presets search up to 16 earlier frames, so their motion vectors can point many frames back and no longer measure the motion since the previous frame. On test set of 27 condition videos, our setting encodes clip in 0.058 s, while the medium and veryslow presets take 5.24 and 21.5 as long, respectively. When x264 is allowed to search 16 frames in the history, 34.5% of the coded P-frame blocks refer to frame that is 2 or more frames back. B-frames. We disable B-frames, which predict blocks from both earlier and later frames. Since B-frame block can take its motion from later frame or average two predictions, its motion vector and residual no longer describe the change since the previous frame. In contrast, with Pframes alone, every motion vector points to the previous frame. With the medium preset, 48.3 of the 70.3 frames in condition video become B-frames on average, and 54.5% of their coded blocks are predicted from later frame. Encoder settings. Each condition is converted from 8-bit RGB to YUV 4:4:4 and encoded once. We use CRF 33 for videos and CRF 35 for images, such that small prediction errors leave no residual. condition of up to 250 frames consists of one I-frame followed by P-frames. The thresholds control the trade-off between the drop rate and the content that the student has to recover. Higher thresholds drop more tokens, including those with small new content that is harder to learn, while lower thresholds retain this content at the cost of lower drop rate. Evaluation setup and metrics This section provides the test data, metrics, and settings of all experiments, organized by base model. C.1. Our multi-condition video model C.1.1. Sampling and pruning We sample our multi-condition model with 30 steps and CFG scale of 3 in Tabs. 1 to 3 and Fig. 5, while Fig. 4 uses its distilled version. We apply threshold-based pruning with the thresholds in Tab. S2 to the Codec (ours) rows of Tab. 1, as well as in Tabs. 2 and 3 and Figs. 4 and S3. In contrast, Fig. 5 drops fixed share of the tokens of each condition through priority-based sorting over all of its tokens. C.1.2. Metrics Video quality. FID [20] is computed on up to 10,000 output frames sampled uniformly from each clip, and FVD [64] on 49 uniformly sampled frames per clip, both against the ground truth. LPIPS [80] compares each output frame with the corresponding ground-truth frame. Before scoring, the frames are resized to 256384 for FID and FVD and to 480640 for LPIPS. In Tab. 2, imaging quality is measured by the MUSIQ [32] score in VBench [24]. Condition following. Each condition metric is computed on the clips that carry this condition. For most conditions, we re-extract the condition from the output with the same extractor that produced the input. For identity, we compute the cosine similarity between the DINOv3 [57] ViT-B/16 class tokens of each identity reference and those of sampled output frames. For segmentation, SAM3 [8] tracks each condition object in the output from its first-frame box, and mIoU averages the IoU over the condition objects. For depth, si-RMSE [12] compares the Video Depth Anything [10] depth maps of the output and the ground truth, while AbsRel in Fig. 5 is computed after aligning the scale and shift per video. For surface normals, we measure the mean angle in degrees between the NormalCrafter [6] normals of the output and those of the ground truth. For edge, we compute the pixel-wise F1 score between the Canny edges of the output and those of the ground truth. For sketch, we compute the SSIM between the Informative Drawings [9] contour drawings of the output and those of the ground truth. For bounding boxes, we compute the AP50 of class-agnostic YOLOv8m detections on the output, which are compared with the condition boxes frame by frame. For blurring, denoted as Deblur in Fig. 5, we compute the PSNR of the output against the ground truth. For inpainting and outpainting, mPSNR is the PSNR over the generated region, i.e., the pixels that the condition leaves empty, and thus excludes the given pixels. For human pose, we compute PCK@0.1 [75] of the Sapiens-1B [34] body keypoints of the people in the output against those of the ground truth. For motion tracks, TrajErr is the mean distance in pixels at 480640 between the requested point tracks and the same points re-tracked on the output with CoTracker3 [31]. For grayscale, E00 is the CIEDE2000 colour difference between the output and the ground truth. Dense tracking, frame interpolation, continuation, and firstframe outpainting have no dedicated metric and are evaluated through FID, FVD, and LPIPS. The metrics for sketch, bounding boxes, and blurring are reported in Fig. 5, and the other condition metrics are reported in Tab. 1. C.1.3. Test cases with more conditions Each test case in Fig. 4 uses different test video, and its conditions are drawn at random from the valid combinations of the training pool, without filtering by quality or results. In these cases, the drop rate depends more on the condition types of case than on their number, since dense appearance conditions drop 5063% of their tokens, while sparse conditions such as motion tracks and bounding boxes drop about 96%. With the KV cache, the keys and values of the condition tokens are reused at every step, so pruning shortens the attention from the noise tokens to these tokens. Without the cache, every step additionally processes all of these condition tokens. C.2. MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA C.2.1. Evaluation dataset details Tab. 4 is evaluated on 237 cases selected from the 813 cases of OmniVBench [37], which cover all seven task families of the benchmark. Since each case requires 50-step generation by both the dense model and CodecOPSD, we focus on cases with long input sequences, which are the main target of codec pruning. Specifically, we rank the cases within each task ID of the benchmark by their number of reference tokens in the DiT and the VLM, as estimated from the inputs. For task families with one, two, and three or more task IDs, we select the top 30, 15, and 10 cases per task ID, respectively, where ties are resolved in favour of less-covered categories. From this selection, we evaluate the cases that both models complete on single H200 GPU. For prompt preparation, MiniMax recommends converting the instruction and references into detailed prompt, with either its online service H3-Context-IR, as used by OmniVBench, or system built on its official prompting guide. We adopt the latter approach and rewrite the prompts with Qwen3-VL-32B [4], whose system prompt is this guide adapted to silent videos. Both models generate videos with the same rewritten prompts and the same seed, while the judge receives the original instructions of the benchmark. S5 C.2.2. Metrics For video quality, we follow the official code of OmniVBench, where technical quality is measured by the DOVER++ [72] technical score, aesthetic quality by the Aesthetic Predictor V2.5 score, and physical plausibility by the physics score of UnifiedReward 2.0 [67]. Reference fidelity and instruction realization follow the official prompts and rubrics and are rescaled to 0100. The benchmark judges these two metrics with Gemini 3.1 Pro, to which we have no API access. Therefore, we adopt the open Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [53] as the judge with the same prompts, large vision-language model with 125B parameters, 6B of which are activated, that natively supports video input. We observe that it provides reasonable understanding of the generated videos for these rubrics. Token drop is defined as one minus the ratio of remaining to dense condition tokens in each case, which is measured before the DiT and, for the reference tokens in the VLM, before its language model. Speedup is defined as the summed denoising time of the dense model divided by that of CodecOPSD. Both are computed per task family, and Overall is the mean over the seven families, following the aggregation of OmniVBench. In Fig. 6 top, quality is the ratio of CodecOPSD to the dense model, averaged over the five metrics. Each video is scored at 480-pixel short side, so that all resolutions are evaluated consistently. C.2.3. Inference settings We use the released 50-step sampler for Tab. 4 and the 8step FastH3-Omni of FastVideo [79] for both the speed and quality measurements in Fig. 6 top. In the DiT, we apply threshold-based pruning to the references, and for reference videos, we further drop part of the remaining tokens through priority-based sorting. In the VLM, we drop the vision tokens with bi = 0 for reference videos. For reference images, we drop the vision tokens that are dropped in the DiT and also fall below quarter of the thresholds. We do not use or compare with KV cache on MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA, since its reference tokens attend to the noise tokens, and we observe that caching their keys and values across denoising steps degrades condition following for both reference images and videos. C.3. MiniMax-H3-Image C.3.1. Evaluation dataset details Tab. 5 is evaluated on all 606 cases of GEdit-Bench-EN [42] and all 400 cases of OmniContext [71]. C.3.2. Metrics The judges of these benchmarks are accessed through APIs. For reproducibility, we instead use the open Qwen3.827B [53] with the official prompts to rate Instr., Consist., and Quality from 0 to 10, so our scores are not comparable to those of the original judges. Instr. measures editing success on GEdit-Bench and prompt following on OmniContext. Consist. measures the absence of over-editing on GEdit-Bench and the consistency of subjects and scenes with the references on OmniContext. Quality is the lower of the naturalness and artifact scores, both of which are rated on the output alone. C.3.3. Inference settings All cases use the official prompt enhancer and the released 6-step sampler. In Tab. 5 and Fig. 6 bottom, we apply threshold-based pruning in the DiT and the image pruning rule of MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA in the VLM. In Figs. S7 and S8, the VLM instead drops the vision tokens that are dropped in the DiT. C.4. Cosmos3-Nano In Tab. 6, the values of the dense model are the mean 2σ over three seeds, and the drop rates of priority-based sorting are selected on the test cases of the table. The denoising speedups in Tab. 6 are measured on one A100 GPU with the released inference pipeline. Note that we observe that the measured speedups also vary with the GPU and inference optimizations. For example, on faster GPUs, the short video-to-action workload is limited by kernel launch overhead rather than computation. C.4.1. Transfer Control-to-video generates 121 frames from single control at 7201280, or at 8321104 for 4:3 clips, and we evaluate 20 selected PAI-Bench-C [83] cases per control. We use the official scorer of PAI-Bench-C, which compares the output with the source video through SSIM for blur, Canny F1 for edge, si-RMSE [12] of estimated depth for depth, and mIoU of SAM 2 [54] masks for segmentation. These scores are not comparable to the metrics of our multicondition model, which re-extract each condition with our own extractors and evaluate blurring with PSNR. Segmentation and depth use threshold-based pruning. For blur and edge, threshold-based pruning moves the quality outside the range of the teacher, so we instead adopt priority-based sorting at the highest tested drop rate that remains within this range, which is 45% for blur and 35% for edge. G. MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA This section extends Sec. 4.5.1 of the main paper with the training details, comparison with Training-Free Codec, and the use of add-on LoRAs and few-step models. G.1. Training details Since the teacher supervises the student on the students own rollout, each training sample consists of the inputs and prompt, and no target output is required. The CodecOPSD LoRA has rank 128, about 655M parameters, and is applied to the condition tokens. It is trained on the 41 tasks in Tab. S8 for 3,000 steps with learning rate of 5 105, where each step supervises one state of 16-step grid. Due to GPU memory limits, each node of 8 GPUs dedicates one GPU to Qwen3-VL-32B [4], the VLM of MiniMaxH3 Ref2VA, and trains on the other seven, resulting in batch size of 14 on 16 GPUs. To save compute, 70% of the training steps generate 56 frames, while the others generate 124 frames. The student receives the reference tokens that remain after threshold-based pruning, and its Qwen3VL drops reference vision tokens with the rule of Supp. C.2. To make the student more robust, part of the training steps further drop some of the remaining reference video tokens through priority-based sorting. Limitations Overall, codec pruning works well across conditions and models, while we also observe few limitations. For motion tracks, codec pruning drops the tokens of point that remains static after the frame where it first appears, so the remaining tokens may confuse static point with an occluded or masked-out one. In addition, few detailed modalities, such as bounding boxes, motion tracks, and blurring, benefit from adjusted codec settings, as listed in Tab. S2. We believe that learning-based search over these settings with pre-computation in advance for each modality is promising direction for future work and may further improve the balance between speed and quality.
